item.title: Fixing GNU Linker Issues: Why Library Order Matters for Symbol Resolution
item.description:
“Fixing GNU Linker Issues: Why Library Order Matters for Symbol Resolution”

When compiling and linking programs, especially those involving static libraries, the sequence in which libraries and object files are presented to the GNU linker drastically impacts whether symbols are correctly resolved. Why does the linker exhibit this strict, order-dependent behavior concerning symbol resolution, and what are the effective strategies for rectifying these dependencies?

The core of the issue lies in how the GNU linker processes input files. It operates as a single-pass linker that does not revisit previously processed libraries once they are consumed for immediate symbol resolution needs.

item.title: C++ Template Linker Errors: Solutions for Explicit Instantiation
item.description:
“C++ Template Linker Errors: Solutions for Explicit Instantiation”

Encountering linker errors with C++ templates, particularly when separating template definitions from declarations, is a common challenge. This often arises when the compiler needs to instantiate a template for a specific type, but the definition isn’t readily available at the point of use. This post delves into various strategies and explanations to address these issues, drawing from established C++ practices and community insights.

item.title: Top 30 Ways to Solve Undefined Reference / Unresolved External Symbol Errors in C++
item.description:
“Top 30 Ways to Solve Undefined Reference / Unresolved External Symbol Errors in C++”

When you compile a C++ program, the process unfolds in several distinct phases. The compiler’s initial task is to transform your source code (.cpp files) into object files (.o or .obj), which contain machine code for the functions and variables defined in that specific source file. During this stage, the compiler simply assumes that any function or variable declared but not defined in the current file will be found elsewhere.
